news.title: North Korea tests AI-powered strategic missile as Seoul-Pyongyang DMZ tensions escalate
news.text:
North Korea tested an AI-linked intermediate-range strategic missile on Saturday, hours after South Korea said Pyongyang had launched a ballistic missile. 

The launch comes days after Seoul’s military demanded an apology from Pyongyang for the DMZ blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul blamed North Korea and the latter denied this responsibility.

Early on Saturday, “our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said. 

“South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defence posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles,” it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometres.

Hours later, North Korea responded to these reports. Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Pyongyang’s leader Kim Jong Un, confirmed that the missile fired in the morning was an “intermediate-range strategic missile”.

She said “the projectile is capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude and AI was introduced into it”, without disclosing the use of artificial intelligence.

North Korea's recent remarks follow leader Kim Jong Un's push to integrate higher levels of artificial intelligence into the nation's weapons. 

Kim Yo Jong boasted that South Korea repeatedly failed to track their missiles whenever Pyongyang utilized a "wave-like trajectory mode." 

Meanwhile, analysts warn that North Korean missile tech may be rapidly improving through Russian assistance. “AI is increasingly being incorporated into military technology worldwide, and ballistic missiles are no exception,” Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs said. 

As per analysts, the launch would be seen as a show of force and act of defiance to South Korea especially at a time when the latter is actively looking to engage in diplomacy with North Korea.
news.author: Aqsa Qaddus Tahir

news.title: North Korea says test of intermediate-range strategic missile included use of AI
news.text:
North Korea said it tested an intermediate-range strategic missile on Saturday that involved the use of AI, hours after Seoul said Pyongyang had launched a ballistic missile.

The launch took place days after Seoul’s military demanded an apology from Pyongyang for a blast that wounded three South Korean soldiers in the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that it blamed on the North.

Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month’s explosion and called South Korea “despicable” on Friday, undercutting overtures by Seoul’s civilian leadership seeking a return to dialogue.

Early on Saturday, “our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea,” Seoul’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.

“South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defence posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles,” it said, adding the missile flew more than 700 kilometres.

Hours later, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Pyongyang’s leader Kim Jong Un, said the missile fired in the morning was an “intermediate-range strategic missile”.

She said the projectile is “capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude and AI was introduced into it”, without elaborating further on the use of artificial intelligence.

She said it meant “there is no way to avoid” the missile’s attack, and claimed Kim Jong Un believed “any country in the world could not have access to such technology for at least several years”.

Her latest statement followed Kim Jong Un’s remarks last month stressing the need to raise “the level of artificial intelligence” in the country’s weapons systems.

Kim Yo Jong claimed that whenever North Korea “applied the wave-like trajectory mode”, South Korea “failed to track the targets from their first skip points”.

Analysts say North Korea could be rapidly advancing its missile technology with Russian military support in exchange for sending troops to support its war against Ukraine.

“AI is increasingly being incorporated into military technology worldwide, and ballistic missiles are no exception,” Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs, told AFP.

“AI can assist with target information and launch operations, while the wars in Ukraine and Iran have shown how linking AI with drones and missiles can enhance their operational effectiveness.”

Hong said it was too early to conclude North Korea’s claims about the missile’s capabilities were accurate.

“North Korea’s missile technology is not particularly advanced compared with leading military powers,” he said. “While missiles that manoeuvre in their terminal phase are difficult to intercept, that does not mean they can strike their targets with perfect accuracy.”

‘Despicable’

Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that last month’s explosion inside the DMZ was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South side of the border.

North Korea’s military has placed mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier as part of efforts to permanently seal it off following leader Kim Jong Un’s designation of South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy” in 2024.

The mines responsible for the blast, which left three soldiers wounded, were believed to have been laid as part of Pyongyang’s border fortification work, according to South Korea’s defence minister Kang Shin-chul.

South Korea’s dovish President Lee Jae Myung had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier.

Kim Yo Jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” on Friday and once again denied Pyongyang was behind the blasts. She ridiculed Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch” and said the military’s demand that her country apologise was “quite ridiculous”.

Kim also warned Pyongyang was “ready for everything” Seoul might do over the mine blast — remarks followed the next morning by Pyongyang’s missile launch.

Analysts said the launch would be viewed as a show of force in response to the South Korean government’s diplomatic efforts, effectively rejecting engagement.

“Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them,” Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP. “The message is that the North is pursuing … confrontation in response to goodwill.”

news.title: N Korea test fires ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology for landmine blast
news.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong said on Saturday that an intermediate-range strategic missile had been tested earlier in the morning, hours after South Korea reported a ballistic missile launch towards the sea.“North Korea's Kim Yo Jong says an intermediate-range strategic missile was used for the drill,” state news agency KCNA reported.Kim Yo Jong, a director of North Korea’s ruling party, said an intermediate-range missile was used in a drill involving a “strategic weapon” towards the sea off the country’s east coast. North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw the drill, carried out by “a firepower sub-unit undertaking an exclusive special mission”, she said, according to Reuters.Citing South Korean and Japanese assessments of the missile’s flight distance, Jong said they showed limitations in tracking capabilities. “Whenever we applied the wave-like trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points,” she said, adding that the weapon could alter its flight orbit at low altitude using artificial intelligence technology.“In other words, this means that there is no way to avoid this attack,” she said.Earlier, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff had said the missile was launched from the Wonsan area on the country's eastern coast and flew more than 700 km (435 miles) towards the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan. South Korean and US militaries were analysing the specifics of the launch.Japan's defence ministry said the missile landed outside the country's exclusive economic zone.The South Korean military said it had strengthened surveillance and vigilance for possible further launches and was closely sharing information with the US and Japan.Seoul's presidential national security office called on Pyongyang to halt its repeated ballistic missile launches, describing them as a violation of UN Security Council sanctions and “a serious act that does nothing to help manage the current situation”.The US Pacific Command said the launch “does not pose an immediate threat to U.S. personnel or territory, or to our allies.”The launch came a day after Kim Yo Jong dismissed South Korean demands for an apology over a September 21 landmine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers near the military demarcation line.South Korea and the US-led UN Command said a joint inspection found that the blast was caused by mines planted by North Korea. The command later said North Korea had violated the armistice agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.Kim Yo Jong rejected Seoul's demands as “utterly pathetic” and said North Korea intended to cut ties with South Korea permanently. In a separate KCNA report, she called Seoul “despicable” and described a proposal by South Korean unification minister Chung Dong-young for border talks as a “wild dream and unilateral jargon”.The latest launch follows a series of North Korean military activities in recent weeks, including missile tests, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship. Wonsan was also the site of a September 20 test that North Korean state media described as involving a hypersonic missile system.South Korean president Lee Jae Myung has urged Pyongyang to return to dialogue, while US President Donald Trump's recent outreach has raised concerns in Seoul about its role in any future nuclear negotiations.North Korea has so far rejected Trump's overtures, saying Washington must first abandon what Pyongyang calls its “hostile policy” and drop denuclearisation as a precondition for talks.
news.author: Subhadra Srivastava

news.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile amid DMZ blast row | Kuwait Times Newspaper
news.text:
SEOUL: North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Saturday, South Korea's military said, days after Seoul demanded an apology for a blast in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that wounded three South Korean soldiers and that it blames on the North. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for last month's explosion. On Friday it called South Korea "despicable", undercutting efforts by Seoul's civilian leadership to restart dialogue.

"Our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan. "South Korea, the US, and Japan are maintaining a robust defense posture through close information sharing regarding North Korean ballistic missiles," it said, adding that the missile flew more than 700 kilometers.

Seoul and the US-led United Nations Command found that the explosion inside the DMZ was caused by North Korean mines laid on the southern side of the border. The heavily mined buffer has divided the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice. North Korea has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the frontier to seal it off permanently since leader Kim Jong Un designated South Korea his country's "principal enemy" in 2024. South Korea's Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul said the mines were believed to have been laid as part of that fortification work.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, a day after his military demanded an apology. Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader, responded on Friday by calling Seoul "really despicable" and again denied that Pyongyang was behind the blast. She ridiculed Lee's overture as "the climax of the farce that everyone should watch" and called the military's demand for an apology "quite ridiculous". She also warned that Pyongyang was "ready for anything" Seoul might do over the incident. The missile launch came the next morning.

Analysts said the launch would be seen as a show of force and an effective rejection of engagement. "Seoul called for easing tensions, but Pyongyang answered by escalating them," Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP. "The message is that the North is pursuing... confrontation in response to goodwill."

On Tuesday, Kang said the military had "a range of necessary measures at our disposal, and we will implement them in stages", without giving details. On Friday, Unification Minister Chung Dong-young proposed talks with Pyongyang on border issues, which Kim Yo Jong dismissed as a "wild dream and unilateral jargon".

The flare-up comes at a sensitive time. US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to Pyongyang have raised concerns that Seoul, a US ally, could be sidelined in any nuclear talks involving the North. On Friday, South Korea's opposition People Power Party accused Lee of failing to criticize Pyongyang when warranted while taking a hard line on Ukraine, which publicly disclosed the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war in an arrangement Seoul believed should be confidential.

"South Korean soldiers have been injured, and far from receiving an apology, we have been mocked by North Korea," the party said in a statement. "We fail to see how selectively turning a blind eye to North Korea serves South Korea's dignity or the safety of its people." — AFP

news.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile toward East Sea
news.text:
North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the East Sea on October 3, with the projectile traveling more than 700 kilometers, according to South Korean military authorities.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missile was detected after being launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea at around 6:30 a.m. local time, or 1:30 a.m. Baku time.

The launch prompted an emergency meeting at South Korea’s National Security Office, where officials reviewed the country’s military readiness and assessed the potential security implications of the latest missile test.

South Korean authorities said they were coordinating with the United States and Japan and exchanging intelligence on the launch.

Japan’s Ministry of Defense also assessed that the projectile could have been a ballistic missile, while Japanese maritime authorities warned vessels to stay away from any possible missile debris.

South Korean officials condemned the launch, saying that North Korea’s ballistic missile tests violate United Nations Security Council resolutions and do not contribute to improving the security situation on the Korean Peninsula.

“We strongly urge North Korea to stop such actions,” the South Korean Presidential Office said.

The latest launch represents another development in North Korea’s ongoing missile activities. According to South Korean military assessments, Pyongyang last conducted a similar launch on September 20.

The launch comes amid continued security coordination between Seoul, Washington and Tokyo over North Korea’s missile and nuclear programs. The three countries regularly share intelligence and conduct military cooperation in response to developments involving North Korean weapons systems.

North Korea has continued to develop and test a range of ballistic missile systems in recent years, prompting repeated criticism from South Korea, Japan, the United States and the United Nations.

The latest projectile was launched toward the East Sea, also known internationally as the Sea of Japan, and South Korean and Japanese authorities continued to assess its trajectory and technical characteristics following the launch.

news.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
news.text:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, ⁠a day ​after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.

The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.

Japan’s ⁠coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been ​a ballistic missile and appeared to have come ‌down, warning ships to take ‌precautions.

South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.

Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, ​issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.

Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.

South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured ⁠three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches ​across the Korean peninsula.

The missile ​test might be an attempt ​by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, ​said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president ‌at the Sejong ​Institute in Seoul, ​a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.

North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.

North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

With Agence France-Presse

news.title: North Korea fires ballistic missile towards East Sea
news.text: Digital Desk | Seoul, Oct 3 (IANS) North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the East Sea on Saturday, South Korea's military said, as tensions heightened over a recent mine blast along the inter-Korean border that injured three South Korean soldiers. The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said it detected the launch at about 6:30 a.m. from the Wonsan area, without elaborating on the type of missile launched. The missile flew over 700 kilometres before landing at sea, the JCS said, adding that it is analysing the exact specifications of the launch with the US side. South Korean and US intelligence authorities had tracked the launch since its early stage and shared relevant information, the JCS said in a notice. "Our military is closely monitoring various movements by the North under a robust South Korea-US combined defence posture and maintaining the capability and readiness to respond decisively to any provocations," it added. While the military did not specify the type of missile, it is reportedly analysing its specifications while leaving open the possibility that it may have been a medium-range ballistic missile (MRBM) or an intermediate-range ballistic missile (IRBM). "There is a possibility that the North fired an IRBM with a reduced range," a government source said, adding the missile appears to be similar to the one launched on August 12. North Korea fired a ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea on August 12 in an apparent protest against the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise between the South and the US, reports Yonhap news agency. The military did not disclose the specifications of the missile at the time, but there was speculation that North Korea may have conducted a reduced-range test launch of an MRBM, with a range of 1,000 to 3,000 kilometres, or an IRBM, with a range of 3,000 to 5,500 kilometres. The latest launch came amid heightened inter-Korean tensions following the September 21 blast of North Korean land mines inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) separating the two Koreas. The incident left three South Korean soldiers injured, two of them seriously. The South Korean military has blamed North Korea for the mine blast, calling it a "blatant violation" of the armistice agreement. Seoul has also demanded an apology from Pyongyang and urged it to halt border fortification work. North Korea denied its involvement in a statement issued Wednesday by Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of its leader Kim Jong-un, accusing Seoul of fabricating the findings and warning of "merciless" retaliation if the South takes any corresponding actions. In a separate statement Friday, Kim again repeated the denial of the North's responsibility, while deriding President Lee Jae Myung's pledge to reduce military tensions between the two Koreas as "the climax of the farce that everyone should watch." She also dismissed Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's proposal for dialogue to discuss the issue of clarifying the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) as a "delusional, one-sided rant not worth responding to." Chung cited the fading visibility of the border line as a primary factor behind the DMZ blast. Saturday's launch came just 13 days after the North fired two short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea within hours of each other on September 20.
news.author: IANS News
